argument: All candidates can be read for slope and intercept; only the first has slope 3 and gives -2 at x=0. The other two violate at least one condition.
Subtracting equations cancels 2x and yields contradiction 4=0. Thus there are zero common points, not a finite positive number.
Both points satisfy x=3. Neither has vertical coordinate 3, and neither satisfies y=x+3, so the alternatives fail direct substitution.
The first equation passes both substitution tests. The second already fails at x=1; the third passes the first point but fails at (3,7), illustrating why both points must be checked.
Parameterise x=t,y=3-t for every real t. Every such point satisfies both equations, and every simultaneous solution has this form.
Their intersection equation is (a-2)x=2. When a=2 it is impossible; for every other a there is exactly one solution 2/(a-2).
For point (u,v), every real m gives y-v=m(x-u), all distinct as m varies; x=u adds the vertical. The theorem of unique line needs two distinct points.
For q≥0, q+10≥10>0, so B is always larger. The algebraic root -10 lies outside the allowed domain and cannot be made positive by discarding its sign.
